# Draft:German colonial aspirations in Southeast Africa

German colonial aspirations in Southeast Africa mainly consisted of private initiatives at the end of the 19th century with the goal to establish German colonies on the Indian Ocean in southern Africa. A parallel development was the founding of what would later become German South West Africa which made a unified German settler colony including multiple regions seem achievable.e. However these plans were in conflict with the colonial interest of Great Britain and German policy at the time was avoiding involvement in this region, so the efforts of land purchase were not protected by the German Empire and failed.
Idea of a German-Boer colony
In his book Vier Jahre in Afrika (Four Years in Africa), published in 1878, the German colonial proponent Ernst von Weber urged Germany to occupy the Delagoa Bay. He directed a memorandum concerning this matter toward the German emperor Wilhelm I and the Imperial Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. Starting from Delagoa Bay, a policy of "Germanization" and patronage was supposed to extend to the German and Dutch settlers of South Africa. These aspirations also failed due to the reluctance of German politics, especially Bismarck's, in colonial matters.
In 1884, Adolf Lüderitz took up von Weber's plan again, as he aspired to expand his founded "Lüderitzland" located in what later turned into German South West Africa all the way to the east up to the Indian Ocean. This territory was meant to include the Boer Republic Transvaal and the resulting colony was intended to be the target for the German emigrant Movements, but these plans were opposed by Bismarck as they expanded way further than patronages for trading posts. Furthermore, Great Britain was working towards installing the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885 following the changing geopolitical circumstances of that region. This protectorate was located between the German Colony in the west and the Boer Republic to the east. Lüderitz felt confined to South West Africa.
In the following years, British disapproval increased due to a German-Boer policy of rapprochement, reaching its climax in 1896 with the Kruger telegram. Before sending out the dispatch, Wilhelm II considered proclaiming the Transvaal republic a German protectorate and sending marines to support the Boers, but abandoned the idea after considering the possible diplomatic and logistical predicaments.
During the 1880s and 1890s, economic interests kept the idea of colonial ambitions in Southern Africa alive, especially focusing on railways, with German investors having taken part in building the Boer railway. Transvaal president Paul Kruger also had plans of constructing a railway stretching from Lüderitz Bay on the Atlantic coast to the Indian Ocean.
Colonial efforts in Southeast Africa
Karl Mauch, a German explorer, travelled to Transvaal and the Mashonaland to speak out in favor of a German colony. During the winter of 1883/84, German colonialist Carl Peters made a proposition to the German foreign office to seize the Mashonaland between Transvaal and the Zambezi. In the following summer, Bismarck declared the territory south of the Zambezi as part of the British sphere of influence, leading to a dismissal of Peters’ proposition. Even the leaders of the German colonial association rejected it unintentionally and prematurely. Peters later complained that the territory was occupied by the British as late as 1889, saying that a German colony would have been possible.
Despite the reluctance of the German government and the competition with Great Britain, German private investors and military personnel initiated isolated preparations for bases in Southeast Africa, none of which, however, persisted. The most advanced project was the attempted occupation of Santa Lucia Bay in Zululand.
Santa Lucia Bay
In November 1884, German traveler August Einwald signed a treaty with King Dinizulu on behalf of Adolf Lüderitz, which was intended to secure a territorial claim for Germany at what is today Lake St. Lucia in the Kingdom of Zululand. The German Colonel Adolf Schiel attempted to assert these supposed claims and the associated possibilities with Bismarck. For a short time, it seemed that a German colony could emerge between Portuguese East Africa in the north and the British colony of Natal in the south. In May 1885, however, the request was finally rejected in the course of a settlement with Great Britain, with the British invoking a treaty that had already been concluded with King Phunga as early as 1843. Between 1884 and 1887, the short-lived Boer state of Nieuwe Republiek was formed around Santa Lucia Bay.
Pondoland
In 1885, the retired First Lieutenant Emil Nagel attempted to establish a German colony in Pondoland. Nagel acquired 400 km² of land from Chief Umquikela. In 1886, Otto Kersten founded the German Pondoland Society in Berlin, which sent an expedition to Pondoland in 1887. The German Pondoland Expedition was tasked with initiating the actual occupation of the land, setting up an experimental station for agriculture and livestock breeding, establishing trade relations with the local residents, and investigating the country's natural resources. The expedition met Usigkao, the son of Chief Umquikela who had passed away in October 1887. After lengthy negotiations, Usigkao confirmed the agreement that had been concluded by his father and E. Nagel. He agreed to the transfer of land to the German Pondoland Society. In 1888, the expedition members built two stations: The station Lambas and the station Intsubana. The station Lambas was situated on the Wild Coast near Port Grosvenor and was used as testing ground for agriculture and livestock farming. The Intsubana station was located further inland in the Ekossa Forest, for collecting wood samples. However, in view of British claims, the German Empire refused it the status of a protectorate. In 1888, Pondoland was annexed by the British Empire. The German Pondoland Society still managed to expand its land holdings to approximately 1500 km² including valuable wood reserves in the Ekossa forest. German newspapers encouraged settlers to alight in these areas, but with little success. In 1894 Pondoland was united with Cape Colony.
Delagoa Bay
The purchase of Delagoa Bay was a repeatedly expressed but never accomplished goal by the German naval and colonial policy. Its strategic position as an access route to the Boer republics once again stoked hopes for a German-Boer land bridge to German South West Africa. The bay, which formerly belonged to Portuguese Mozambique, was of great interest to England, Germany, and the Boer republics during the 1890s. The railway connecting Pretoria and the harbour of Lourenço Marques in the Delagoa Bay was partially funded by German capital. To secure access to the harbour and railway for Germany, the Imperial German Navy dispatched warships to the bay to the opening of the railway in 1895. The cruisers Condor and Cormoran signaled Germany's presence in the bay, with the aim of pressuring the British Empire into making concessions regarding the expected redistribution of the Portuguese colonies, which did not happen at first.
